Wikipedia 'Battles of Khalkhin Gol' (citing Krivosheev 2001, Coox 'Nomonhan: Japan Against Russia, 1939'); ww2db.com
notes: Own/enemy strength (57,000 vs 25,000) is a matched late-August 1939 snapshot; Japanese total committed over the whole campaign is cited separately as high as 75,000. own_casualties uses Krivosheev's revised 25,655 (9,703 dead/missing + 15,251 wounded + 701 sick) over Zhukov's own contemporaneous report of 9,284 -- a nearly 3x gap, and the same 'reject the self-serving commander's own figure in favor of a modern archival revision' standard already used for Caesar's Commentarii elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_casualties uses Japanese Sixth Army medical records (19,714) over the Soviet wartime propaganda claim of 52,000-61,000 Japanese dead, on the same reject-the-inflated-claim logic used against Juvaini's Samarkand toll for Genghis Khan. opponent_general_id is Komatsubara (23rd Division commander, whose division was actually encircled and destroyed) rather than Ogisu (Sixth Army's nominal overall commander, appointed only in the campaign's final phase).

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Yelnya offensive' (citing Glantz & House, 'Barbarossa Derailed'); Warfare History Network 'Meat Grinder at Yelnya'
notes: Zhukov's first personal field command of the war (Reserve Front, formed 1 Aug 1941), and the first Soviet recapture of German-held territory in the war. own_troop_strength (70,000) is single-sourced to Warfare History Network -- Wikipedia/Glantz give no isolated Reserve Front/24th Army strength figure. enemy_troop_strength (103,200, Glantz & House 1995 p.293) conflicts with Warfare History Network's much lower ~60,000 estimate for the same German force, a real unresolved ~40%+ discrepancy; Glantz's figure is used as the more rigorously cited one. own_casualties (31,853 = 10,701 killed/missing + 21,152 wounded) and enemy_casualties (23,000) both per Glantz & House, covering the broader Aug 8-Sept 8 window their tables use rather than the narrower Aug 30-Sept 8 offensive-proper dates. Glantz notes the 24th Army lost nearly 40% of its operational strength here, despite which the battle is coded Strategic rather than Pyrrhic given its outsized propaganda/morale value as the first Red Army victory of the war.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Moscow' (citing Glantz & House 'When Titans Clashed', Krivosheev 'Soviet Casualties and Combat Losses', Reinhardt); Warfare History Network 'Zhukov Strikes Back'
notes: Zhukov took command of the Western Front on 10 Oct 1941, 8 days into the battle as dated here; own_troop_strength (1,252,591) is the 1 Oct theater snapshot (Western+Reserve+Bryansk Fronts combined), the earliest whole-theater figure found -- no source isolates Western Front strength alone. Figures used for the whole battle (defense phase to 5 Dec, counteroffensive to 7 Jan) combine multiple fronts (Western under Zhukov, Kalinin under Konev from 17 Oct, Southwestern under Timoshenko) rather than Zhukov's command in isolation; Zhukov is credited with the whole battle here as the dominant/senior field commander directing the defense of the capital, the same 'personally supreme-directed' standard already used for Grant's Overland Campaign (Meade held formal tactical command, Grant strategic direction) elsewhere in this dataset. own_casualties (1,029,234) sums Krivosheev's defense-phase (658,279) and counteroffensive-phase (370,955) figures. enemy_casualties (174,194) is the German official monthly-tracked total Oct 1941-Jan 1942; a separate, less precisely sourced range of 250,000-400,000 German dead/wounded also appears in the literature and is flagged rather than used, since it likely reflects a broader Barbarossa-to-Moscow date window rather than the battle proper. Clodfelter reportedly scopes 'Battle of Moscow' more narrowly (15 Nov-5 Dec 1941, the German final push only) -- a genuine definitional-scope disagreement about what counts as 'the battle', separate from the casualty-count disagreements above, flagged here rather than resolved.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Operation Mars' (citing Glantz 1999 'Zhukov's Greatest Defeat', Krivosheev 1997, Beevor 2012, Grossmann 1980, Beshanov, Isayev, Buttar 2022)
notes: Zhukov's most significant personal defeat, jointly commanding Western Front (his own) and coordinating with Kalinin Front against Model's 9th Army; per Glantz, personally directed rather than a Stavka-coordinator role, unlike the Stalingrad/Kursk/Bagration exclusions elsewhere in this roster. own_casualties is the single most contested figure in this dataset: Krivosheev's official Soviet figure is 215,674 (70,373 irrecoverable + 145,301 wounded/sick); Beshanov gives ~250,000; Glantz's revised estimate (the namesake of his book, arguing Soviet-era figures were deliberately minimized because Mars was a clear failure unlike the simultaneous Stalingrad counteroffensive) is 100,000 killed + 235,000 wounded = 335,000, roughly 55% above Krivosheev's figure. Glantz's revision is used here, following the same 'prefer the modern historian's corrective over the self-serving/official lower figure' standard already applied to Caesar's Commentarii and Khalkhin Gol above. own_troop_strength (702,923) is the more specific Wikipedia infobox figure for Mars itself; a broader ~1.4 million figure covering the whole simultaneous Rzhev-Sychevka operation complex (including Operation Jupiter) is not used since it is not specific to Mars. decisiveness left blank per this schema's convention for a Loss with no clean single label -- the Soviet force was checked and took catastrophic losses but did not break, similar to Grant's Cold Harbor/Second Petersburg elsewhere in this dataset.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Vistula-Oder offensive'; Wikipedia 'Josef Harpe'
notes: Figures are the combined total of Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front and Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front jointly executing this offensive; despite a targeted search, no source was found isolating Zhukov's own front's strength or casualties separately from Konev's. Documented and combined rather than fabricating a split, the same treatment as Caesar's Alesia and Saladin's Siege of Acre combining multi-force totals into one field elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_troop_strength (450,000) is the lower end of a 450,000-800,000 cited range for Army Group A; the wider figure may include reinforcements/replacements fed in during the offensive rather than initial strength. Gen. Josef Harpe held Army Group A command for most of the offensive before being relieved on 20 Jan 1945 specifically for failing to stop it, replaced by Ferdinand Schörner; Harpe is recorded as opponent_general_id as the commander actually opposed for most of the fighting.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Seelow Heights' (citing Isaev 2010; Hastings 2005 p.468; Beevor 2002 p.244; Le Tissier 1996 p.273)
notes: The one battle in this roster with troop-strength figures cleanly isolated to Zhukov's own 1st Belorussian Front (1,000,000, including 78,556 of the Polish 1st Army) against a single named opposing formation (Busse's German 9th Army, 112,143) rather than a multi-front combined total. own_casualties is a genuine, large historian dispute: Isaev (Russian archival) gives 5,000-6,000 killed/missing out of ~20,000 total casualties; Hastings and Beevor separately cite ~30,000 killed. Isaev's total-casualty figure (20,000) is used since it matches this field's definition; Hastings/Beevor's number is killed-only and not directly comparable, so is flagged rather than substituted -- the disagreement is preserved, not resolved by picking whichever number is lower. enemy_casualties (12,000, Hastings) is likewise killed-only, likely an undercount of total casualties, but no other figure was found. political_constraint_flag=true reflects Stalin's deliberate creation of a competitive race between Zhukov's and Konev's fronts to reach Berlin first, redrawing the inter-front boundary mid-offensive to spur speed -- widely cited by historians as a contributing factor in Zhukov's costly frontal-assault approach here. The wider 'Battle of Berlin' (the April 16-May 2 city-assault operation, of which Seelow was the opening battle) is deliberately excluded as a separate row: its only available figures are a three-front (Zhukov + Konev + Rokossovsky) combined total for the whole period, which would substantially double-count the same 16-19 April forces and casualties already captured in this row. Unlike the Vistula-Oder/Alesia-style 'combine multi-force figures into one field and document it' treatment used elsewhere, this is a direct date/force overlap with an already-included row, so exclusion is the more honest choice here than double-counting the same soldiers into career totals.

source_citation: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Georgian Chronicles); Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History of Armenia; Timothy May, The Mongol Art of War; Wikipedia 'Battle of Khunan'
notes: Co-commanded with Jebe as joint primary decision-makers on an independent reconnaissance-in-force Genghis Khan authorized after the Khwarazmian pursuit reached the Caspian -- same 'co-equal senior partner' standard already documented for Jebe/Subutai jointly in this dataset's Genghis Khan rows is extended here to Subutai's own roster, since no source subordinates either man to the other for this campaign. Troop strength (30,000 Mongols and allies vs. 30,000 Georgian-Armenian coalition) is the figure given for the battle itself; the campaign opened with smaller forces (20,000 Mongol / 10,000 Georgian) that both grew before the decisive engagement. Casualties are only described qualitatively in every source found ('moderate' Mongol, 'heavy' Georgian) -- own_casualties and enemy_casualties here are order-of-magnitude placeholders consistent with that language, not source-given counts, the same treatment given to several Genghis Khan/Saladin rows elsewhere in this dataset. Feigned-retreat envelopment tactic (classic Jebe/Subutai playbook, also used at Kalka the following year). King George IV of Georgia was mortally wounded in the chest and died of the wound on 18 January 1223; recorded as opponent_general_id as the coalition's named royal commander (atabeg Ivane Mkhargrdzeli also present but not senior to the king).

source_citation: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh; Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History of Armenia; Timothy May, The Mongol Art of War; Wikipedia 'Battle of Khankala (1222)'
notes: Fought weeks/months after Khunan in the same 1222 North Caucasus campaign, same Jebe/Subutai joint-primary command as that row. Opposing coalition (North Caucasians -- Alans, Durdzuk/Vainakh, Circassians, Lekia -- plus Kipchak Turks) was won over by first bribing the Kipchak contingent to abandon the field, then destroying the remainder; Durdzuk forces broke out and escaped the encirclement, the one incomplete part of an otherwise total victory. own_troop_strength uses 25,000 as a round mid-estimate for the infobox's 'fewer than 30,000'; enemy_troop_strength (~50,000) is the coalition figure before the Kipchak defection thinned it. No source gives a specific casualty count for either side -- only 'moderate' Mongol losses against a coalition 'almost entirely wiped out,' with captured survivors reportedly executed; own_casualties and enemy_casualties are order-of-magnitude placeholders on that qualitative language, same treatment as the Khunan row. Two coalition leaders are named ('Yuri', a Cuman/Kipchak chief, wounded; 'Daniel') with no clear single supreme commander identifiable across a multi-ethnic coalition, so opponent_general_id is left blank, the same convention used for Genghis Khan's Zhongxing/Yehuling rows elsewhere in this dataset.

source_citation: Novgorod First Chronicle; Galician-Volhynian Chronicle; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Kalka River'
notes: The best-attested Jebe/Subutai joint-command battle in the sources, and the culmination of the same reconnaissance-in-force campaign as Khunan/Khankala -- treated here as the anchor battle of Subutai's roster. own_troop_strength (23,000) combines the modern-estimated 18,000-20,000 Mongols with their Brodnici (Slavic frontier) allies, who fought alongside them rather than against them. enemy_troop_strength uses 33,000, the midpoint of modern estimates' 20,000-45,000 range for the Rus'-Cuman coalition, rejecting the chronicle claim of up to 80,000 -- same 'prefer the modern historian's corrective over the inflated chronicle figure' precedent already used for Caesar/Genghis/Hannibal elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_casualties (73,000, the midpoint of the commonly cited 70,000-75,000 dead/wounded/captured/missing/deserted/executed figure, 'only every tenth man returned to Rus'') is unusually large relative to even the high end of the troop-strength estimate -- sources reconcile this by folding in the rout and multi-day pursuit slaughter after the battlefield collapse, not battlefield dead alone; flagged here since it is a real feature of the sources, not a data-entry inconsistency. own_casualties ('minor' in every source, no hard figure) is an order-of-magnitude placeholder. Six Rus' princes were killed; Kievan Grand Prince Mstislav III of Kiev, the coalition's senior named commander, was captured and executed (reportedly suffocated under a platform the Mongol commanders then feasted on) -- recorded as opponent_general_id over the more tactically active Mstislav Mstislavich of Galicia, since Mstislav III held the senior princely title.

source_citation: Rogerius of Apulia, Carmen Miserabile; Yuan Shi; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Battle of Mohi'
notes: Fought under Batu Khan's nominal supreme command of the western campaign, but this is the strongest-documented case in the sources of Subutai as the real tactical author despite a nominally senior prince -- the Yuan Shi states outright 'everything achieved then was due to Subutai's merit,' and the post-battle political dispute (Guyuk and Buri accusing Batu of riding Subutai's coattails to victory) directly names Subutai's role over Batu's, a more direct textual basis than exists for several other Batu-era candidate battles researched and dropped from this roster (see generals.csv note). political_constraint_flag=true for this reason: Subutai held real tactical authority but only nominal subordinate rank beneath a Chinggisid prince, a genuine, well-documented constraint on his formal command authority, not merely normal chain-of-command hierarchy. own_troop_strength (30,000) follows Sverdrup's estimate of 'at least 30,000' engaged, toward the high end of the wide 15,000-30,000 contemporary-source range; enemy_troop_strength (25,000) follows the modern-favored estimate over Juvaini's chronicle claim of roughly double the Mongol force, same inflated-chronicle rejection as the Kalka River row. enemy_casualties (10,000) is the contemporary-source figure (the Western European Epternacher Notiz); later secondary summaries citing up to 40,000-80,000 likely conflate battlefield/pursuit losses with the subsequent countrywide devastation of Hungary, so the more conservative contemporary figure is used. own_casualties has no reliable consensus in any source ('several hundred to several thousand') -- 1,500 is an order-of-magnitude placeholder, not a source-given count; Carpini later reported seeing a large Mongol war-dead cemetery from the campaign in Russia, confirming real but unquantified losses. Effectively ended organized Hungarian resistance for the rest of the year. resource_backing_tier=4, one step above the Caucasus-campaign rows: this is the main western campaign under the reigning Great Khan Ogedei's authorization with the empire's full mobilization behind it, versus the earlier rows' cut-off reconnaissance-in-force.

source_citation: Yuan Shi; Jin Shi; Richard Gabriel, Subotai the Valiant; Wikipedia 'Siege of Kaifeng (1232)'
notes: Ogedei sent two armies to converge on the Jin capital, one under his own nominal command and one under his brother Tolui; once the two forces joined, command passed to Subutai, who led the siege throughout, becoming sole commander for its final phase after Tolui fell ill and died and Ogedei withdrew -- an unambiguous personal-command case, unlike the nearby Battle of Sanfengshan (Feb 1232, the field battle that preceded this siege and destroyed the Jin's last army), which this roster excludes: Wikipedia's own battle-specific article credits Tolui as the tactical planner with Subutai unmentioned, while other sources credit Subutai -- a genuine, unresolved command-attribution split (documented in generals.csv) that this dataset's personal-command bar treats as excludable, the same standard already applied to Zhukov's Stavka-coordinator battles elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_troop_strength (300,000, commonly cited as the Jin defense force: ~120,000 regulars, ~100,000 irregulars, ~80,000-100,000 auxiliaries) is very likely inflated by garrison/auxiliary padding the way several other sieges in this dataset are (cf. Genghis's Yehuling/Zhongxing rows), but no specific modern recount was found to correct it against, so the commonly cited total is used rather than an unsourced guess. enemy_casualties (150,000) is a deliberate downward correction from the commonly repeated 'approximately 95% of the defense force' (~285,000) claim, which implies near-total destruction of an already-inflated force estimate -- the same skepticism already applied to Juvaini's Samarkand death toll in Genghis Khan's roster. Separately, and explicitly excluded from this row's casualties fields since the schema defines them as military losses: an estimated 40-50% of the city's roughly one-million civilian population died from the siege, subsequent famine, and a documented plague outbreak during the 1233 truce negotiations -- a real, separately attested demographic catastrophe, not folded into enemy_casualties here to avoid conflating civilian and military losses. own_casualties (5,000) is an order-of-magnitude placeholder for real but unquantified Mongol losses during the prolonged siege, including the Jin defenders' documented early use of gunpowder 'thunder-crash bomb' weapons (Jin Shi); no source gives a specific Mongol death toll. Jin Emperor Aizong fled the city before its fall (recorded as opponent_general_id, the Jin state's supreme authority throughout the siege) and the city was surrendered by the Han defector general Cui Li rather than stormed; decisiveness=Strategic rather than Rout since the siege ended in a political collapse/flight rather than the destruction of a field army, and the Jin dynasty itself did not fall outright until the follow-on Siege of Caizhou in 1234 (outside this campaign and not personally led by Subutai as far as this research found).

source_citation: Atkinson, An Army at Dawn: The War in North Africa, 1942-1943 (Henry Holt, 2002); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; cross-checked against Wikipedia 'Operation Torch' infobox
notes: Eisenhower's first Allied supreme command (Allied C-in-C, Allied Expeditionary Force, appointed Aug 1942); no peer coordinator above him, matching the 'singular top of the chain' standard used for Grant/Zhukov elsewhere in this dataset. own_casualties (1,967 = 556 US dead + 837 US wounded + 574 UK dead) omits a UK-wounded figure not found in any source, so likely undercounts true Allied losses -- flagged rather than estimated. opponent_general_id is Nogues (Vichy French Resident-General in Morocco, the senior military authority across French North Africa) over Darlan (the political figure who negotiated the ceasefire and switched sides on 14 November, mid-battle) or Juin (Algiers-specific field commander) -- a genuinely fragmented, three-way command on the opposing side, noted since no other row in this dataset has quite this structure. political_constraint_flag=true for the 'Darlan Deal': Eisenhower personally authorized the ceasefire-for-recognition agreement with the Vichy French admiral, ending organized French resistance within days but provoking a political firestorm in Washington/London he had to personally defend.

source_citation: Atkinson, An Army at Dawn (2002); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; cross-checked against Wikipedia 'Tunisian campaign' infobox and historyofwar.org
notes: Own/enemy troop strength (500,000/350,000) is a March 1943 mid-campaign snapshot, the earliest whole-campaign figure found; enemy_casualties (290,000, low end of a cited 290,000-362,000 range) is dominated by the mass Axis surrender on 13 May 1943 (238,000-300,000 captured, sometimes compared in scale to Stalingrad -- 'Tunisgrad' in the literature), the basis for coding decisiveness=Rout despite the campaign's rocky start. Includes the Kasserine Pass defeat (19-24 Feb 1943, Anderson/Fredendall's tactical loss, no Eisenhower decision documented for the battle itself) within this single campaign-level row rather than excluding or splitting it out, since Eisenhower's own decisive response -- personally relieving Fredendall (replaced by Patton, then Bradley) and bringing in Alexander to unify fragmented ground command as 18th Army Group commander -- happened within days and is arguably stronger evidence of personal command than most of Torch. opponent_general_id is von Arnim (Army Group Afrika, commanded through the final surrender) over Rommel (relieved for health on 9 March 1943, partway through the campaign) as the single defensible opponent for a campaign-spanning row; Rommel commanded the opposing Axis forces through Kasserine specifically. political_constraint_flag=true for the Darlan assassination (24 Dec 1942, mid-campaign) and the awkward Giraud/de Gaulle succession politics that followed, which Eisenhower had to personally manage alongside the military campaign.

source_citation: D'Este, Bitter Victory: The Battle for Sicily, 1943 (Dutton, 1988); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; cross-checked against Wikipedia 'Allied invasion of Sicily' infobox
notes: The weakest personal-command case in this roster, flagged rather than silently included: AFHQ (Eisenhower) sat above 15th Army Group (Alexander, ground command), Patton's Seventh Army, and Montgomery's Eighth Army; documented evidence of Eisenhower personally making decisive calls (as opposed to approving Alexander/Montgomery/Patton's plans and arbitrating their Messina-race rivalry) is thinner here than anywhere else in the roster. Included anyway on the same 'theater-level approval/arbitration counts as supreme command' standard used for Torch/Tunisia, but with political_constraint_flag=false -- unlike this roster's other rows, the Montgomery-Patton rivalry Eisenhower arbitrated here reads as ordinary inter-Allied friction, not the externally-imposed political interference the other rows document. own_troop_strength (160,000 initial invasion force, rising to a 467,000 peak not used here) and enemy_troop_strength (250,000, combining Italy's ~200,000 engaged of a wider 131,359-252,000-personnel range plus Germany's 40,000-60,000) are both flagged approximations given wide source ranges. own_casualties (24,900 = US 9,968 + UK/Canada 14,932) and enemy_casualties (181,970 = Italy 154,039 + Germany 27,931, dominated by mass Italian captures) sum the Wikipedia infobox's own national breakdowns. decisiveness=Strategic (Mussolini's fall days after the campaign, opening the invasion of the Italian mainland) despite the well-documented Allied failure to seal the Straits of Messina before ~100,000 Axis troops evacuated to the mainland -- D'Este's title itself ('Bitter Victory') reflects this real tactical shortfall inside a strategic win.

source_citation: Ambrose, D-Day: June 6, 1944 (Simon & Schuster, 1994); Atkinson, The Guns at Last Light: The War in Western Europe, 1944-1945 (Henry Holt, 2013); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; cross-checked against Wikipedia 'Operation Overlord' infobox and Britannica's 'Estimated Battle Casualties During the Normandy Invasion and Campaign to Liberate Paris'
notes: The pre-dawn 5 June 1944 D-Day go/no-go decision, made on Group Captain Stagg's weather brief, is the single most unambiguously personal command decision in Eisenhower's whole war -- no subordinate could have made it. But per the SHAEF plan, Eisenhower delegated ground command of the entire Allied force (both British 21st Army Group and US First Army, not one army under one subordinate) to Montgomery for the whole lodgement/breakout period, only assuming direct personal ground command on 1 Sept 1944 -- a materially bigger delegation than the Grant/Meade precedent this dataset otherwise relies on, flagged here as this general's single biggest judgment call rather than resolved by analogy alone. own_casualties (209,935 = US 124,394 + UK ~65,000 + Canada 18,444 + Poland 2,097) carries its own internal vintage disagreement: the wartime G-3 tally gives 20,668 US killed for this window, a 1953 US Adjutant General revision gives 29,198 for the same dates -- flagged, not resolved. enemy_casualties (320,000, Britannica citing US Army official histories: 30,000 killed/80,000 wounded/210,000 missing, >70% of missing later confirmed captured) is used over the raw infobox's '~80,000 killed, 233,000 captured' split, which Wikipedia itself flags as source-disputed. decisiveness=Rout reflects the German Seventh Army/Panzer Group West being rendered combat-ineffective as formations by campaign's end, not merely defeated in the field. Falaise Gap (12-21 Aug, a Bradley decision with no Eisenhower decision documented) is excluded as a separate row since its dates fall entirely inside this row's 6 Jun-30 Aug window and would double-count troops/casualties already captured here -- the same principle as Zhukov's Seelow Heights/Battle of Berlin exclusion. Operation Market Garden (Sep 1944, Montgomery's own conception and execution, approved under coalition-political pressure rather than directed by Eisenhower) is excluded from the roster entirely on the same Stalingrad-style no-documented-decision basis.

source_citation: Beevor, Ardennes 1944: The Battle of the Bulge (Viking, 2015); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; MacDonald, A Time for Trumpets (William Morrow, 1985); cross-checked against Wikipedia 'Battle of the Bulge' infobox
notes: The strongest personal-command case in this roster: within ~24 hours of the 16 Dec surprise attack, Eisenhower personally committed SHAEF's only theater reserve (82nd and 101st Airborne, refitting after Market Garden) to plug the gap and hold Bastogne, before the offensive's full scale was understood. At the 19 Dec Verdun conference he personally set the strategic framing ('the present situation is to be regarded as one of opportunity for us and not of disaster') and directed Patton to disengage Third Army and wheel north -- Patton's famous reply is a direct response to an Eisenhower question at that meeting. On 20 Dec he personally placed US First and Ninth Armies under Montgomery's operational control for the northern shoulder, a hugely controversial decision among American commanders (especially Bradley), reversed once the salient was reduced. own_troop_strength (705,000, the 2 Jan peak) and enemy_troop_strength (449,000, the 24 Dec peak) are matched near-peak snapshots rather than the 16 Dec opening figures (228,741/406,342), which are noted here for contrast. own_casualties (90,900 = US DoD figure of 89,500 [19,000 killed/47,500 wounded/23,000 missing], the figure most consistently attributed to Clodfelter's tables, + ~1,400 British) and enemy_casualties (100,000, a round mid-estimate between the German High Command's own contemporaneous 81,834-98,024 and the US wartime estimate of 103,900) both carry real, unresolved cross-source ranges, flagged rather than false-precision resolved. political_constraint_flag=true covers both the political fallout from the offensive's initial intelligence-failure surprise and the coalition-politics controversy over the temporary Montgomery command arrangement, worsened by Montgomery's tactless 7 Jan 1945 press conference that Eisenhower had to personally defuse.

battle_name: Western Allied invasion of Germany (Rhine crossing and final drive)
source_citation: D'Este, Eisenhower: A Soldier's Life (Henry Holt, 2002); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; cross-checked against Wikipedia 'Western Allied invasion of Germany' and 'Ruhr pocket' infoboxes
notes: Eisenhower's own decisive personal calls in this phase are strategic rather than operational -- the three actual river crossings (Montgomery's Operation Plunder in the north, Bradley's opportunistic exploitation of the captured Remagen bridge in the center, Patton's and Devers' crossings in the south) were each a subordinate army-group commander's own execution; Eisenhower does not even appear in Plunder's own Wikipedia command list. His documented personal decisions instead: rejecting Montgomery's repeated single-thrust-to-Berlin proposals in favor of the broad-front strategy (a running dispute documented in D'Este), and the SCAF 252 telegram sent directly to Stalin communicating the decision to halt the Western advance at the Elbe and let the Red Army take Berlin -- made largely outside normal Anglo-American political channels and provoking a real Churchill dispute (hence political_constraint_flag=true, which also covers the Jan 1945 Strasbourg/de Gaulle crisis just before this row's date range, where Eisenhower's initial order to withdraw from Strasbourg was reversed after de Gaulle threatened to pull French forces out of SHAEF command). own_troop_strength/enemy_troop_strength (4,500,000/1,600,000) and own_casualties (106,145 = US 62,704 + French 18,306 + UK 17,930 + Canada 6,490 + other 715) are the infobox's own campaign totals. enemy_casualties is the one figure in this row needing a documented compromise rather than a clean citation: the infobox's own '265,000-400,000 killed' range is explicitly scoped to 'all fronts,' not the west alone, so is not used; no single source was found reconciling a total West-front German killed+wounded+captured figure for the full 22 Mar-8 May window. enemy_casualties instead uses the single largest, well-documented, genuinely West-specific capture event inside it -- the Ruhr Pocket's ~317,000 POWs, surrendered 14-18 Apr 1945, the largest single German surrender in Western Europe in the war -- with the explicit caveat that this is a lower bound and excludes casualties from Operations Veritable/Grenade/Plunder/Lumberjack and the final collapse elsewhere in the West. source_confidence=Low, the only Low-confidence row in this roster, specifically because of this gap -- the same 'document the gap rather than fabricate a number to fill it' standard used for several Genghis Khan/Saladin/Hannibal rows elsewhere in this dataset. opponent_general_id is Kesselring (OB West from 10 March 1945, replacing von Rundstedt, in command through the final surrender) over Model (Army Group B, encircled in and died by suicide inside the Ruhr Pocket on 21 April) since Kesselring held the senior theater command across this row's full date range.
